## II. Boston (1848–1854)

Peter Chardon Brooks, the other grandfather, died January 1, 1849, bequeathing what was supposed to be the largest estate in Boston—about two million dollars—to his seven surviving children. The Adams connection was singularly small in Boston, but the family of Brooks was singularly large and almost wholly of clerical New England stock. One might have sought long in much larger societies for three brothers-in-law more distinguished than Edward Everett, Dr. Frothingham, and Charles Francis Adams. One might have sought equally long for three men more unlike. Mr. Adams stood most apart. Almost alone among his Boston contemporaries, he was not English in feeling or sympathy. He could have taken his inherited rights of political leadership in succession to Webster and Everett; but instead, he drew himself aloof and renewed the old war against the slave-power which had already lasted since 1700. He could not help it. With the record of J. Q. Adams fresh in popular memory, his son could not make terms with the slave-power, and the slave-power overshadowed all the great Boston interests. His children were anti-slavery by birth, as their name was Adams and their home was Quincy. Had State Street been Paradise, they must hunger for it in vain, and it hardly needed Daniel Webster to act as archangel with the flaming sword to order them away from the door.

The year 1848 was like enough to 1776 to make a fair parallel. The parallel was complete when, a few months after the death of John Quincy Adams, a convention of anti-slavery delegates met at Buffalo to organize a new party and named candidates for the general election in November: for President, Martin Van Buren; for Vice-President, Charles Francis Adams.

For any American boy the fact that his father was running for office would have dwarfed every other excitement. But beyond personal bias, the year 1848 was decisive for twenty years to come. The stamp of 1848 was almost as indelible as the stamp of 1776—with this difference: men whose lives were to fall between 1865 and 1900 had first to get rid of it, and take the stamp that belonged to their own time. This was their education. The old Puritan nature rebelled against change. Nature had given the boy Henry a character that in any previous century would have led him into the Church; he inherited dogma and *a priori* thought from the beginning of time; and he scarcely needed a violent reaction like anti-slavery politics to sweep him back into Puritanism with the force of a religious war.

His father's character was therefore the larger part of his education, and for that reason the son was always a much interested critic of his father's mind and temper. To his son Henry, the quality that distinguished his father from all the other figures in the family group was that, in his opinion, **Charles Francis Adams possessed the only perfectly balanced mind that ever existed in the name.** For a hundred years, every newspaper scribbler had derided or abused the older Adamses for want of judgment. They abused Charles Francis for his judgment. Charles Francis Adams was singular for mental poise—absence of self-assertion or self-consciousness—the faculty of standing apart without seeming aware that he was alone—a balance of mind and temper that neither challenged nor avoided notice, nor admitted question of superiority or inferiority, of jealousy, of personal motives, from any source, even under great pressure. This unusual poise, ripened by age, became the more striking to his son as he learned to measure the mental faculties themselves, which were in no way exceptional for depth or range. His memory was hardly above the average; his mind was not bold like his grandfather's or restless like his father's, nor imaginative nor oratorical. But it worked with singular perfection, admirable self-restraint, and instinctive mastery of form. Within its range it was a model.

Never once in forty years of intimacy did his son notice in him a trace of snobbishness. He was one of the exceedingly small number of Americans to whom an English duke seemed indifferent, and royalty itself nothing more than a slightly inconvenient presence. Never did his son see him flatter or vilify, or show a sign of envy or jealousy; never a shade of vanity or self-conceit. The critics charged him with the opposite defect—they called him cold. No doubt such perfect poise was not maintained by nature without a sacrifice of the qualities that would have upset it. Had his nature been cold, he would have followed Webster, Everett, and Seward in the lines of party discipline and self-interest. Had it been less balanced, he would have gone with Garrison, Wendell Phillips, and Theodore Parker into secession. Between the two paths he found an intermediate one, distinctive and characteristic—he set up a party of his own.

This political party became a chief influence in the boy Henry's education between 1848 and 1854. The group associated with Mr. Adams, whose social centre was the house in Mount Vernon Street, numbered only three: Dr. John G. Palfrey, Richard H. Dana, and Charles Sumner. Palfrey was the oldest, and in spite of his clerical education was often the most agreeable, for his talk was lighter and his range wider. Dana affected to be still before the mast—a bluff, vigorous seaman—but as one knew him better one found a man of rather excessive refinement deliberately hardening his skin to the burden, as though he were still carrying hides at Monterey. His mind worked close to its subject, as a lawyer's should; but disguise and silence it as he liked, it was aristocratic to the tenth generation.

Sumner was altogether out of line with the other three. He too adored English standards, but his ambition was to rival the career of Edmund Burke. No young Bostonian of his time had made so brilliant a start. The Free Soil Party fared ill in Beacon Street, and Sumner was socially ostracized—as were Palfrey, Dana, and Adams—but for them it mattered less because they had houses and families of their own. Sumner had neither wife nor household, and though the most socially ambitious of all, and the most hungry for polite society, he could enter hardly half-a-dozen houses in Boston. His solitude was glacial, and reacted on his character. The boy Henry worshipped him. Sumner was the boy's ideal of greatness; the highest product of nature and art. To the twelve-year-old boy, his father and Dana and Palfrey were men, more or less like what he himself might become; but Sumner was a different order—heroic.

As the boy grew up, his father gave him a writing-table in an alcove of the Boston library, where, winter after winter, Henry worked over his Latin Grammar and listened to these four gentlemen discussing anti-slavery politics. Mr. Adams had undertaken to edit a newspaper as the organ of the group, and they came to discuss its policy and expression. He was also editing the *Works* of his grandfather John Adams and made the boy read texts for proof-correction. The boy got as little education fitting him for his own time from the one task as from the other, and no more from his contact with the gentlemen themselves, who were all types of the past.

Viewed from Mount Vernon Street, the problem of life was as simple as it was classic. Politics offered no difficulties, for there the moral law was a sure guide. Education was divine, and man needed only a correct knowledge of facts to reach perfection. Nothing quieted doubt so completely as the mental calm of the Unitarian clergy. They proclaimed as their merit that they insisted on no doctrine, but taught the means of leading a virtuous, useful, unselfish life, which they held sufficient for salvation. Boston had solved the universe; the problem was worked out.

Of all the conditions of his youth which afterward puzzled the grown-up man, **this disappearance of religion puzzled him most.** The boy went to church twice every Sunday; he was taught to read his Bible; he believed in a mild deism; he prayed; he went through all the forms; but neither to him nor to his brothers or sisters was religion real. Even the mild discipline of the Unitarian Church was so irksome that they all threw it off at the first possible moment and never afterward entered a church. The religious instinct had vanished, and could not be revived, although one made many efforts in later life to recover it. That the most intelligent society, led by the most intelligent clergy, in the most moral conditions he ever knew, should have solved all the problems of the universe so thoroughly as to have quite ceased making itself anxious about past or future, seemed to him the most curious social phenomenon he had to account for in a long life. In religion and philosophy no one protested. Such protest as was made took forms more simple than the silence—the deism of Theodore Parker, or the less aggressive withdrawal of Emerson, which was, from an old-world point of view, merely naïf.

The children reached manhood without knowing religion, and with the certainty that dogma, metaphysics, and abstract philosophy were not worth knowing. So one-sided an education could have been possible in no other country or time; it became, almost of necessity, the more literary and political. The boy soon became a desultory reader of every book he found readable—commonly eighteenth-century historians, because his father's library was full of them. He read shelves of eighteenth-century poetry; but when his father offered his own set of Wordsworth as a gift on condition of reading it through, the boy declined. Pope and Gray called for no mental effort; but he was thirty years old before his education reached Wordsworth.

He always reckoned his school-days, from ten to sixteen, as time thrown away. For success in the life imposed on him he needed, as afterward appeared, the facile use of only four tools: Mathematics, French, German, and Spanish. These he never controlled. Latin and Greek he could have learned more thoroughly in six weeks of intelligent adult effort than in the six years spent on them at school. Thus, at the outset, he was condemned to failure more or less complete in the life awaiting him. On the whole, the happiest hours of the boy's education were passed in summer lying on a musty heap of Congressional Documents in the old farmhouse at Quincy, reading *Quentin Durward* and *Ivanhoe*, and raiding the garden at intervals for peaches and pears. On the whole he learned most then.
